Make Your Own Website

HTML like it’s 2005

Filed under: Blog
11/vi/2026

Making your own website is simpler than it might seem and it’s a nice alternative to putting your work up for the world to see on increasingly monetised social media platforms. What’s more, having your own website grants you an exceptional amount of control over it. You can change the style as you see fit, not just within the confines of what’s imposed by FaceBook or Twitter or Tumblr. You can make your text

very large and red

or very small and blue; you can use Small Caps With a Wavy Underline, you can use custom emojis that invert colours when you hover over them etc. etc. In short, you can break any and all stylistic guidelines, written or unspoken, and there’s no-one to stop you.

Contrary to what you might think, you can also host a website for free. In the course of this article, I’ll try to teach you — the, presumably, uninitiated reader — the basics of creating a webpage. Note that this is targeting recreational, unprofessional webpage creation. This is not a comprehensive guide to web design, not even close. It’s more of “learn to write HTML like it’s 2005” kind of article.

So, let’s begin with a brief explanation of how webpages work and then an introduction into writing them, piece by piece.

What is a website, anyway?

Let’s say you open your browser and go to a website, say, https://example.com. Your browser will look at that URL and understand that it needs to contact the server called “example.com” and ask for its index, which is sort of like the homepage. When it does so, the server responds by communicating that everything went properly and sends an HTML file containing the code of the webpage, which will contain references to CSS files which define the styling to apply (all text should be in Arial, tables should have a 1 pixel wide border etc.) and Javascript files, little programs that say how the webpage is supposed to behave (what should happen when I click on this button, what happens when the user minimises the browser etc).

Like a JPEG file or a PNG file encode how an image is supposed to look, HTML encodes the contents of a webpage. Unlike JPEG and PNG, however, HTML files are meant to be readable and writeable by humans, which means that you can open them in a text editor and you should be able to understand them with no issue. HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. The word “markup” is significant; unlike regular programming languages, which tend to very strict about their structure, markup languages treat anything that doesn’t have its special characters as regular text.

You can try this out for yourself. Open a text editor — I don’t mean a word processor like Microsoft Word or LibreOffice Writer, but an actual text editor like Notepad or Sublime Text. Then copy the code below in it:

Code 
Hello, world!

This is my webpage.
Preview
Hello, world! This is my webpage.

Save this file as file.html and double-click it (or go to your browser and choose File > Open File). You should see something similar to what’s in the Preview section above. There you go, you have just made an (admittedly very simple) webpage! You will have noticed that the webpage you’ve just made ignored the whitespace and put the text on one line. That’s because HTML makes no assumptions. You have to tell it what you want it to display. Otherwise, it will interpret anything you give it in the exact same way: as text with un-important whitespace. Writing HTML will be the subject of the following section.

Writing HTML

How do we structure our webpage, then? The most important thing to know when writing HTML are tags. Tags can be paired, like the <p> tag, which is used to mark up a paragraph. In code, we just write the opening tag <p> before the beginning of the paragraph and a closing tag </p> after the end. These tags (<p> and </p>) create a p element. An element is a unit in the abstract model of our web page that the browser creates. Tags are just the sequence of characters that tell the browser displaying our web page: “This is where the element’s content begins and this is where it ends.” Let’s change our webpage slightly:

Code 
<p>Hello, world!</p>

<p>This is my webpage.</p>
Preview

Hello, world!

This is my webpage.

The <p> tags tell the browser to create two paragraph elements, one after the other. Some tags, like the line-break tag, don’t need to be paired. All we need to do is to write <br> where we want to break the paragraph in two lines. This tag is unpaired, so there’s no need for us to close it with a corresponding </br> tag.

Code 
<p>Hello, world<br>and all who inhabit it!</p>

<p>This is my webpage.</p>
Preview

Hello, world
and all who inhabit it!

This is my webpage.

Historically, unpaired tags used to be written with a slash before the > character, so the line break tag would be written as <br/> or <br />. This style is still valid, but isn’t favoured anymore.

We can give our document a sense of structure with the <h1>, <h2>, <h3>, <h4>, <h5> and <h6> elements. <h1> creates a level 1 heading, <h2> creates a level 2 heading, and so on.

Code 
<h1>My document</h1>
<p>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.</p>

<h2>Section 1</h2>
<p>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.</p>

<h2>Section 2</h2>
<p>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.</p>
Preview

My document

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.

Section 1

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.

Section 2

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.

To introduce a thematic break, we can use the <hr> (horizontal rule) element. Much like <br> (defined above), <hr> is unpaired; don’t write a closing </hr> tag after it. <hr> will make a line:

Code 
<p>Upon waking in her room, Joanna felt a strange feeling of emptiness. Her husband was dead. There was nothing else she had to do.</p>

<hr>

<p>Police Commissioner Konstanz had an uneasy night.</p>
Preview

Upon waking in her room, Joanna felt a strange feeling of emptiness. Her husband was dead. There was nothing else she had to do.

Police Commissioner Konstanz had an uneasy night.

For quoting things, the <blockquote> element is quite handy. Generally, you should put the quoted content inside of paragraph elements too.

Code 
<p>A wise man once said:</p>

<blockquote>
    <p>“Because bread tastes better than key.”</p>
    <p>– Wise Man.</p>
</blockquote>
Preview

A wise man once said:

“Because bread tastes better than key.”

– Wise Man.

Throughout the article, we’ll sometimes use comments in the code to explain things. Comments start with <!-- and end with -->. They aren’t visible to the user. They’re essentially little notes left by programmers for themselves or for other programmers.

Code 
This is text <!-- and this is a comment --> and this is more text.
Preview
This is text and this is more text.

Attributes and links

Another thing we need to talk about before we get into more complicated examples are attributes. Sometimes, we need to add additional information to a element. A good example are links: in HTML, these are called anchors and are created using the <a> element. An anchor needs two things to be functional: a text to display and a URL to bring the user to when clicked. The text is simply what’s written between the opening <a> and the closing </a>. The URL is indicated using the href attribute:

Code 
<p>
    <a href="https://youtube.com">This is a link to YouTube</a>.
</p>
Preview

This is a link to YouTube.

As you can see, an attribute is written as NAME="VALUE". Don’t forget the quotes. The code can work without them, but it might break in some circumstances. Also, specifically when it comes to the href attribute, you can’t just write href="youtube.com". Your browser needs the whole URL, otherwise it will assume that youtube.com is the name of a file somewhere else on the website and clicking the anchor will take you there.

Anchors can also take another attribute: target. When used with the value of target="_blank", the link will open the URL in a new tab:

Code 
<p>Clicking on <a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">this link</a> will open https://example.com in a new tab. When you wish to return to this article, simply close the tab.</p>
Preview

Clicking on this link will open https://example.com in a new tab. When you wish to return to this article, simply close the tab.

Links can also be used to move around a document, not just from one document to the next. For this, we need to specify an id attribute on the element we want to jump to and link to it with an <a> element. So, if we want to create a link to a heading, for example, we’ll write it as <h1 id="my-heading">. Then, if we want to link to it somewhere else in the document, we write <a href="#my-heading">. Notice that the id attribute doesn’t contain a hashtag, but the href attribute does. This is perfectly logical: id="my-heading means “the ID of this element is my-heading,” while href="#my-heading" means “this link will jump to an element on this same page with the ID (#) of my-heading.”

Code 
<h1 id="main-title">Main Title</h1>

<p>Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text.</p>

<a href="#main-title">Jump back to main title</a>
Preview

Main Title

Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text. Some text.

Jump back to main title

Some attributes can also be specified without a value. For example, the hidden attribute can be used on any element and will prevent it from being shown to the user. This is not that useful, but it can come in handy in specific circumstances. Here’s an example of how to use it:

Code 
<p>This is my first paragraph. The user is meant to see it.</p>
<p hidden>This is my second paragraph. The user is NOT meant to see it.</p>
<p>This is my third paragraph. This one should be seen.</p>
Preview

This is my first paragraph. The user is meant to see it.

This is my second paragraph. The user is NOT meant to see it.

This is my third paragraph. This one should be seen.

hidden and id are global attributes, which means they can be used with any elmenent. Other attributes, like align, can only be used on specific elements. align controls the alignment of the element. Possible values are left (default), right and center.

If you want to align multiple paragraphs to the centre, you could add align="center" to each one. An alternative is to put them inside of a <div> element with align="center". <div> (content division) is used to group content together for styling purposes.

Code 
<h1 align="center">My Amazing Title</h1>

<p>My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text.</p>

<div align="center">
    <p>We have nothing to fear... but fear itself.</p>
    <p>– FDR</p>
</div>
Preview

My Amazing Title

My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text. My amazing text.

We have nothing to fear... but fear itself.

– FDR

Typesetting elements

Now we have gone over the most important aspects of HTML syntax. We have only seen a couple of elements so far though, so let’s take a look at a few others. Firstly, <em>, short for “emphasis,” which is used to display important text. By default, it just makes the text render in italics. Here is an example:

Code 
<p>This is one of the <em>worst</em> marketing campaigns I had ever seen!</p>
Preview

This is one of the worst marketing campaigns I had ever seen!

Similarly, <strong> puts strong emphasis on what’s inside. Let’s see an example again:

Code 
<p>
    AI-isms aren’t just <em>annoying</em>, they’re <strong>insufferable</strong>—some might even say <strong><em>unforgivable</em></strong>.
</p>
Preview

AI-isms aren’t just annoying, they’re insufferable—some might even say unforgivable.

Among the other font-related elements are <u>, used for underlining text, <s>, which strikes the text out, and <mark>, which highlights the text in yellow. Furthermore, there’s <sup> for superscript text (like powers: 22) and <sub> for subscript (like in chemical formulae: H2SO4). Here’s an example that puts them all together:

Code 
<p>
    Your suggestion regarding CO<sub>2</sub> emissions is <s>weclo</s>
    <u>welcome</u> and we look forward to our next collaboration.
    We will contact you around <mark>October 19<sup>th</sup></mark>.
    Would that be OK with you?
</p>
Preview

Your suggestion regarding CO2 emissions is weclo welcome and we look forward to our next collaboration. We will contact you around October 19th. Would that be OK with you?

More typesetting with the <font> element

The <font> element (now deprecated) can be used to customise the font of its content. It has three attributes: face, which customises the font family, color, which can be a hexadecimal RGB colour or one of the many named colours, and size, which is a value from 1 (smallest) to 7 (largest). 3 is the default. You can also add a + or -, so that +2 in the below example means “2 sizes larger than the current font size.”

Code 
<div align="center">
    <h1><font color="red">WARNING!</font></h1>
    <p>
        <font color="blue" face="Arial" size="2">
            This website is <br>
            <font color="purple" size="+2"><em>still under construction!</em></font>
        </font>
    </p>
</div>
Preview

WARNING!

This website is
still under construction!

Creating lists

To create a bullet list, use the <ul> (“unordered list”) element. Each <li> (“list item”) element inside is going to represent a single bullet point.

Code 
<p>This is my shopping list. It doesn’t need to be ordered, so I’m going to use an unordered list:
<ul>
    <li>eggs</li>
    <li>milk</li>
    <li>bread</li>
    <li>olive paté</li>
</ul>
Preview

This is my shopping list. It doesn’t need to be ordered, so I’m going to use an unordered list:

  • eggs
  • milk
  • bread
  • olive paté

A numbered list is created in much the same way, except you use the <ol> (“ordered list”) element. As with bullet lists, each list item is represented with the <li> element.

Code 
<p>Let’s rank my favourite books:</p>
<ol>
    <li><em>Don Quixote</em> by Miguel de Cervantes.</li>
    <li><em>Moby Dick</em> by Nathaniel Hawthorne.</li>
    <li><em>Pale Fire</em> by Vladimir Nabokov.</li>
</ol>
Preview

Let’s rank my favourite books:

  1. Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes.
  2. Moby Dick by Nathaniel Hawthorne.
  3. Pale Fire by Vladimir Nabokov.

We can also change the first number of the list using the start attribute:

Code 
<p>Now let’s rank my least favourite of the 9999 books I’ve read:</p>
<ol start="9997">
    <li><em>The Vindication of Eternity</em> by Jaromír Hladík</li>
    <li><em>The Concrete Garden</em> by Ian McEwan</li>
    <li><em>Milk and Honey</em> by Rupi Kaur</li>
</ol>
Preview

Now let’s rank my least favourite of the 9999 books I’ve read:

  1. The Vindication of Eternity by Jaromír Hladík
  2. The Concrete Garden by Ian McEwan
  3. Milk and Honey by Rupi Kaur

An individual list item’s value can also be changed using the value attribute:

Code 
<ol start="9998">
    <li><em>The Vindication of Eternity</em> by Jaromír Hladík</li>
    <li><em>The Concrete Garden</em> by Ian McEwan</li>
    <li value="1"><em>Milk and Honey</em> by Rupi Kaur (it’s so bad it loops around to being good)</li>
</ol>
Preview
  1. The Vindication of Eternity by Jaromír Hladík
  2. The Concrete Garden by Ian McEwan
  3. Milk and Honey by Rupi Kaur (it’s so bad it loops around to being good)

Sometimes you want the numbered list to use roman numerals instead. Or maybe capitalised letters of the Latin alphabet. These options are controlled by the type attribute. Its possible values are 1 for Arabic numberals (1, 2, 3...), i and I for lowercase and uppercase Roman numerals (i, ii, iii... and I, II, III... respectively) and a and A for lowercase and uppercase letters of the Latin alphabet (a, b, c... and A, B, C... respectively).

Code 
<ol>
    <li>
        One thing we haven’t mentioned yet is that lists can be nested. This is useful when:
        <ol type="a">
            <li>You have more to say.</li>
            <li>You have more to say.</li>
            <li>You have more to say.</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li>
        Another thing we should mention is that you can use multiple attributes at the same time.
        <ol type="A" start="4">
            <li>This allows you to continue the list we started above...</li>
            <li>...and add more things!</li>
        </ol>
    </li>
    <li type="i">
        Hopefully you’ll never use this, but you can also change the numbering of an individual list element!
    </li>
    <li type="I" value="99">
        All this is to say, <strong>HTML</strong> is really cool!
    </li>
</ol>
Preview
  1. One thing we haven’t mentioned yet is that lists can be nested. This is useful when:
    1. You have more to say.
    2. You have more to say.
    3. You have more to say.
  2. Another thing we should mention is that you can use multiple attributes at the same time.
    1. This allows you to continue the list we started above...
    2. ...and add more things!
  3. Hopefully you’ll never use this, but you can also change the numbering of an individual list element!
  4. All this is to say, HTML is really cool!

Tables

A table is created with the appropriately named <table> element. Each row is within a <tr> (table row) element. Each row can consist of an arbitrary number of <td>’s (table data, i.e. normal table cells) or <th>’s (table header).

Code 
<p>Our study yielded the following data:</p>

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Tetris high score</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>18</td>
        <td>50</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Anne</td>
        <td>21</td>
        <td>83</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Adele</td>
        <td>33</td>
        <td>120</td>
    </tr>
</table>
Preview

Our study yielded the following data:

Name Age Tetris high score
John 18 50
Anne 21 83
Adele 33 120

The above example works fine, but, especially for tables that are part of a document, it’s recommended to provide a caption using the <caption> element. You can use the align attribute to align the caption on the "left", "right", "top" or "bottom". You can also use rules="groups" to show a border on the top and bottom of the table.

Code 
<table rules="groups">
    <caption align="bottom">Data revealed in our study</caption>
    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Tetris high score</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>John</td>
        <td>18</td>
        <td>50</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Anne</td>
        <td>21</td>
        <td>83</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Adele</td>
        <td>33</td>
        <td>120</td>
    </tr>
</table>
Preview
Data revealed in our study
Name Age Tetris high score
John 18 50
Anne 21 83
Adele 33 120

In the olden days, before proper styling support, tables were often used to define page layout (as an example, see this website on Shevchenko’s poems). Nowadays, this style isn’t favoured anymore, but for beginners it can be a useful way to define headers, footers and the like, especially with the help of the colspan and rowspan attributes of <td> and <th>. colspan="3" means “this cell will take up 3 columns,” while rowspan="2" means “this cell will take up 2 rows.”

You will notice we also use the <big> and <small> element in the example below. They are self-explanatory (<big> makes what’s inside larger and <small> makes it smaller). We also use the bgcolor attribute to change the background colour of the left sidebar and the valign element to control the vertical alignment (top, middle or bottom).

Code 
<table>
    <tr>
        <!-- Left sidebar -->
        <td rowspan="3" valign="top" bgcolor="lightgrey">
            <a href="#">Home</a>
            <a href="#">Articles</a>
            <a href="#">About</a>
        </td>
        <!-- Header -->
        <th colspan="2"><big>My website’s logo</big></th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <!-- Main content -->
        <td>
            <h1>My article</h1>
            <p>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.</p>
        </td>
        <!-- Right sidebar -->
        <td rowspan="2" valign="top">
            <p>Related websites:</p>
            <a href="#">johnblow.com</a>
            <a href="#">picturesofcats.com</a>
            <a href="#">bayareanews.com</a>
        </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <!-- Footer -->
        <td><small>This website was created by <a href="#">me</a> in A.D. 2026.</small></td>
    </tr>
</table>
Preview
Home Articles About My website’s logo

My article

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet.

Related websites:

johnblow.com picturesofcats.com bayareanews.com
This website was created by me in A.D. 2026.

Images and figures

So far, we’ve only talked about text, but a big part of the web’s appeal is the ability to include images. Images are created with the <img> element. This tag, like <br>, is unpaired, so there’s no need for a closing </img> tag. The source URL of the image is provided in the src (source) attribute. You should get into the good habit of providing alt text using the alt attribute. This text is displayed if the image URL is incorrect and is also used by screen readers to help visually-impaired users understand what the image represents. By default, the image is displayed in its actual size, which is usually too large; use the width and height attributes to control its size.

Code 
<img
    src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg/960px-%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg"
    alt="A drawing of a lion."
    width="350">
Preview

Be careful about what images you put on your website! If they are copyrighted, you could get in trouble. The above image is from Wikimedia Commons and is licensed under the extremely permissive Creative Commons Zero license.

Many websites like to take you to the image source when you click on it. This can be done by wrapping the <img> element in an <a> element:

Code 
<a href="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg/960px-%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg">
    <img
        src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg/960px-%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg"
        alt="A drawing of a lion."
        width="350">
</a>
Preview

An out of context image isn’t too nice on your users. For this reason, HTML has the <figure> element. By using it and specifying a caption using the <figcaption> element, you can provide some additional context to the displayed image:

Code 
<figure>
    <a href="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg/960px-%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg">
        <img
            src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg/960px-%22_A_Lion%22%2C_Folio_from_a_Dispersed_Nuzhatnama-i_%E2%80%98Ala%E2%80%99i_of_Shahmardan_ibn_Abi%E2%80%99l_Khayr_MET_DP240347.jpg"
            alt="A drawing of a lion.">
    </a>
    <figcaption>A Lion, Folio from a Dispersed Nuzhatnama-i ‘Ala’i of Shahmardan ibn Abi’l Khayr (MET, 13.160.8)</figcaption>
</figure>
Preview

As you will have noticed, the <figure> element has the added benefit of constricting the size of the image, so we don’t have to specify the width attribute anymore!

Leaning into the old web aesthetic

As said at the beginning, this is a guide to creating simple websites in the old style. One unmissable aspects of the old web aesthetic are

marquees!

The <marquee> element isn’t good practice in modern web design, but can still be charming when used sparingly.

If you don’t do well with a lot of moving objects, you might want to skip to the next section.

Code 
<marquee>
    WARNING! Your Computer Caught A Virus!
</marquee>
Preview
WARNING! Your Computer Caught A Virus!

With attributes, you can control the direction (direction="left", "right", "up" or "down"), behaviour (behavior="scroll", "slide" or "alternate") and speed.

Code 
<marquee behavior="slide">Sliding marquee (will stop)</marquee>
<marquee behavior="scroll">Scrolling marquee (won’t stop)</marquee>
<marquee behavior="alternate">Alternating marquee (won’t stop)</marquee>

<!-- This should show a 2D bouncing DVD logo.
     It doesn’t work on all browsers. -->
<marquee behavior="alternate" direction="down" width="200" height="200">
    <marquee behavior="alternate">
        <em>DVD</em>
    </marquee>
</marquee>

A proper website

Now, it’s finally time to use the above described tags and create an actual, presentable website. If we put the website content and save it as index.html, it will certainly work. But such a website will have no metadata and isn’t very professional. We should adhere to the required HTML document structure. We’re going to need to use this basic structure:

Code 
<!-- <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser that the document is written in
    HTML5 and not any earlier version. Most browsers assume this anyway,
    but including it is still good practice. -->
<!DOCTYPE html>

<!-- <html> is the root tag of the whole document. The `lang` attribute
    specifies the language (en for English, de for German, fr for French
    etc. -->
<html lang="en">

<!-- The head contains the metadata of the webpage. -->
<head>
    <!-- Title of the webpage. You can’t use any tags inside. -->
    <title>My Website</title>

    <!-- This line makes your webpage look much better on phones. -->
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
</head>

<!-- The body contains the actual content of the webpage. -->
<body>
    <!-- Our page content goes here. -->
</body>

</html>

All we need to do is to fill in the relevant blanks, write our content and look at the webpage we’ve just made in the browser! Here is an example to get you started:

Code

                <p>A frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura. Frog species with rough skin texture due to wart-like parotoid glands tend to be called toads, but the distinction between frogs and toads is informal and purely cosmetic, and does not reflect taxonomy or evolutionary history.</p>

                <h2 id="frog-etymology">Etymology</h2>
                <p>The origins of the word <em>frog</em> are uncertain and debated. The word is first attested in Old English as <em>frogga</em>, but the usual Old English word for the frog was <em>frosc</em>, and it is agreed that the word frog is somehow related to this. Old English <em>frosc</em> remained in dialectal use in English as frosh and frosk into the nineteenth century, and is paralleled widely in other Germanic languages, with examples in the modern languages including German <em>Frosch</em>, Norwegian <em>frosk</em>, Icelandic <em>froskur</em>, and Dutch <em>(kik)vors</em>.</p>

In the former, adopted by the majority of species, adult frogs at certain times of year assemble at a pond, lake or stream to breed. In explosive breeders, the first male that finds a suitable breeding location, such as a temporary pool, calls loudly and other frogs of both sexes converge on the pool. Explosive breeders tend to call in unison creating a chorus that can be heard from far away.</p>

Table of Contents

  1. Etymology
  2. Reproduction

Frog

A frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura. Frog species with rough skin texture due to wart-like parotoid glands tend to be called toads, but the distinction between frogs and toads is informal and purely cosmetic, and does not reflect taxonomy or evolutionary history.

Etymology

The origins of the word frog are uncertain and debated. The word is first attested in Old English as frogga, but the usual Old English word for the frog was frosc, and it is agreed that the word frog is somehow related to this. Old English frosc remained in dialectal use in English as frosh and frosk into the nineteenth century, and is paralleled widely in other Germanic languages, with examples in the modern languages including German Frosch, Norwegian frosk, Icelandic froskur, and Dutch (kik)vors.

Reproduction

Two main types of reproduction occur in frogs, prolonged breeding and explosive breeding. In the former, adopted by the majority of species, adult frogs at certain times of year assemble at a pond, lake or stream to breed. In explosive breeders, the first male that finds a suitable breeding location, such as a temporary pool, calls loudly and other frogs of both sexes converge on the pool. Explosive breeders tend to call in unison creating a chorus that can be heard from far away.

Made to be shared

This alone is a pretty fun way to spend an afternoon and you could theoretically send the .html file to your friends and get them to open it in their browser, but you can actually put it online for free. There are multiple services that will host your website (this website is hosted on GitHub Pages), but the most user-friendly one is Neocities. Sign up, press the red “Edit Site” button and upload your file, or write it directly in the browser! The whole point of the web is that it’s all in plain sight. If you want to check out the way someone else’s website works, right-click the web page and press “Inspect.” This will show you the page’s source code. Now hack around all you’d like; that’s the way you learn. On Safari, inspecting the site’s source code is a little more complicated.

Big sites like Facebook, Twitter or Youtube rely on very sofisticated web applications running on a server that automatically generate a webpage for the given request. These web pages are called dynamic, since they are generated on the fly in order to reflect things like the number of likes, the number of subscribers (for Youtube), followers (for Twitter) or friends (for Facebook), the comments and replies, etc. In contrast, services like Neocities and Github Pages allow only static web pages: this means you don’t need to create a web application that would generate an HTML file on the fly (which would be fairly complicated, both for you as the user and for the service). Let’s say you name your Neocities website xyz. When someone opens xyz.neocities.org/about.html (your website’s URL), Neocities will see if there’s a file called about.html on your website. If not, it will serve either a default “not found” web page or a custom one (on Neocities it’s called not_found.html). If a folder is requested, the server will send the index.html file. If you want your URLs to be cleaner, you can create a folder called about and place the content of the “about” page in a file called about/index.html. Now the URL of the “about” page is going to be xyz.neocities.org/about/.

That’s all for now. There are many more things to be learned about HTML and about the rest of web design. You will notice that most websites (including this one) don’t really look like the websites we created here. That’s because as websites got more and more complex, there arose a need to distinguish between style and semantics. According to this distinction, modern HTML should communicate only the structure of the web page, not how it’s supposed to look. The style is left to a separate language, CSS (Cascading Style Sheets), which goes beyond the scope of this article. If you’d like to learn more about HTML, check out the MDN Web Development tutorials or the less serious Neocities tutorials. If you don’t remember what exactly an element does, it’s always a good idea to look it up on the MDN Html Element Reference.
